nodes.question: How were the open questions in the survey analyzed?
nodes.answer: Two members of the team conducted thematic analysis separately to identify key themes related to the open questions.
nodes.paragraph: Our inclusion criteria were: HIA practitioners, academics, educators or commissioners or other relevant HIA experience (self-identified). The sur - vey asked the following: the participant S current role, country currently based in, background in and experi - ence of HIA, their views on important areas of research for HIA, the priority research questions and how to build and support HIA research, what they think the research needs are and how we could support the development of HIA research over the next 10 years. The closed questions were descriptively analysed. Two members of the team (FH and MD) separately carried out thematic analysis of the open questions to identify key themes in relation to the questions; What do you think the most important areas of research needed in the field of HIA in the next ten years? What do you think the most important unresolved research questions in HIA are? How can we build and support HIA research? What are important factors/ next steps/ approaches that we should be considering? The research team met to discuss these and resolve any difference in themes identified.

nodes.question: What timeframe was established for the survey's availability?
nodes.answer: The survey was open for 14 weeks, specifically from August to December 2022.
nodes.paragraph: Development in HIA research is needed to address gaps and advance the field. Methods - approach to developing the research agenda To develop a research agenda for HIA, we followed sev - eral steps using a mixed method approach to data and evidence collection including a survey, and qualitative interactive workshops [ 30] (see Fig. 1). Data collection Phase 1: Developing ideas Phase 1 involved an international survey of HIA practi - tioners. We developed a short anonymous self-admin - istered online survey using the Qualtrics platform (see Haigh et al. BMC Public Health (2025) 25:791 supplementary document 2). Ethical approval was granted by University of New South Wales Human Ethics Advisory Panel (HC220581). An invitation to complete the survey was circulated through existing email net - works including the HIANET, the International Associa - tion for Impact Assessment HIA section, the European Public Health Association HIA Section, Society of Prac - titioners of HIA, and the International Union for Health Promotion and Education Global Working Group on HIA. The survey was open for 14 weeks between August and December 2022.

nodes.question: What time period did the random sample survey take place?
nodes.answer: The survey was conducted from July 19 to July 25, 2024.
nodes.paragraph: Aba Prefecture is a severe cold area, as shown in Fig. 3. In this study, the traditional houses of Yueli Village, Wenchuan County, Aba Prefecture, were selected as the research object rather than the famous traditional settlements, which can better reflect the universality and authenticity of the research. Questionnaire A random sample survey of long-term residents of Yueli Village, Wenchuan County, Aba Prefecture was carried out from July 19 to July 25, 2024 to evaluate the indoor environment of traditional houses. 135 questionnaires were issued, and 123 valid questionnaires were returned. The data are representative and can objectively reflect residents feelings about the indoor thermal environment. The interview content involves residents thermal comfort in the indoor environment, including the number of permanent residents, gender, age, living habits, construction area, building materials, etc. During the interview, respondents were asked about indoor temperature, humidity, air quality, and whether they felt cold, hot, stuffy, wet, and other symptoms. Respondents were also asked whether they used fans, air conditioners, or other equipment to regulate indoor temperature and humidity.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Democratic practices|Public opinion surveys_qna_005
nodes.label: Methodology
nodes.question: What methods were used to analyze the data collected from the survey?
nodes.answer: Data analysis was conducted using simple summative scoring with a point system for rankings and a rank-ordered logit model to explore preferences for the sample and subgroups.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Objective As societies emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic, governments are increasingly moving away from a focus on economic growth at any cost towards the principles of a wellbeing economy, focused on achieving a more equitable distri- bution of wealth and wellbeing. This study aimed to assess the relative importance to the Australian general public of the key principles of a wellbeing economy and to investigate heterogeneity in preferences between demographic subgroups. Methods An online survey was developed and delivered to a general public sample of 2042 Australian adults (aged 18 years and above). Respondents were invited to rank the key principles of a wellbeing economy (dignity, nature and climate, social connection, fairness and participation) plus two additional traditional economic indicators of societal success ( economic growth and economic prosperity ) in order of their relative importance for informing future policy directions. Data analysis was conducted using simple summative scoring, which involved the use of a point system allocated to rankings as a depend- ent variable. In addition, a rank-ordered logit model was used to explore preferences for the entire sample and subgroups defined by key socio-demographic characteristics.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Democratic practices|Public opinion surveys_qna_006
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What was the context in which the survey was conducted?
nodes.answer: The survey was conducted during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
nodes.paragraph: Results Dignity (people have enough to live in comfort, safety and happiness) and fairness (equal opportunity for all Australians and the gap between richest and poorest greatly reduced) were ranked as the most important priorities for the total sample and for key socio-demographic subgroups differentiated by age, level of education and level of socio-economic advantage. Traditional economic indicators of societal success including economic prosperity and economic growth were considered important but generally ranked below the principles of dignity and fairness Conclusions The findings indicate that government movements away from traditional economic indicators and towards new broader wellbeing economy measures of societal success are likely to be supported by the general public. * Rachel Milte rachel.milte@flinders.edu.au Matthew Crocker matthew.crocker@flinders.edu.au Gang Chen gang.chen@monash.edu Gordon Duff g.duff@unsw.edu.au Julie Ratcliffe julie.ratcliffe@flinders.edu.au 1 Health and Social Care Economics Group, Caring Futures Institute, Flinders University, Adelaide, GPO Box 2100, Adelaide, SA 5001, Australia 2 Centre for Health Economics, Monash University, Caulfield East, Melbourne, VIC 3145, Australia 3 Public Service Research Group, UNSW Canberra, Canberra, ACT 2600, AustraliaKey Points for Decision Makers The principles of dignity and fairness were the two most important priorities identified by Australians to guide policy in our survey conducted during the corona- virus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Democratic practices|Public opinion surveys_qna_011
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: According to Luca Ausili, what are the political risks associated with the quantification of information by political leaders?
nodes.answer: The political risks include the misconception that numerical data are objective, the potential exclusion of non-quantifiable issues from political debate, and the resulting disillusionment and distrust from the populace.
nodes.paragraph: It contains a series of papers all previously selected through a double-blind peer-review process presented at an international workshop with the same title, held in Milan on September 11 and 12, 2023, at the University Vita-Salute San Raffaele, and organized by the European Centre for Social Ethics (ECSE). The articles in this volume revolve around several major thematic lines. The first concerns the quantity, quality, and nature of the information that circulates, especially on the Internet, and from which socially relevant and sometimes dangerous phenomena emerge, as they can influence indi - vidual decisions. The second addresses the way in which information is created and disseminated and how it ulti - mately reaches specific targets. The third part deals with the normative consequences of the current knowledge crisis scenario for both individuals and institutions. In The Political and Socio-Epistemic Risks of Quanti - fication, Luca Ausili reflects on the growing tendency of political leaders to make use of empirical data to quantify information in an attempt to convey objectivity and rational - ity qualities inherently associated with numbers. Express - ing themselves through the use of quantified data betrays political leaders need to make the information they com - municate appear unbiased and impersonal.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Democratic practices|Public opinion surveys_qna_012
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: According to Luca Ausili's article, what is a significant risk associated with the pursuit of quantification in political discourse?
nodes.answer: A significant risk is that not all numerical data are objective, which can lead to the exclusion of important qualitative issues from political debate, resulting in disillusionment and distrust among the population.
nodes.paragraph: But, as Ausili argues, the assumption that numbers are truly an expression of neutrality and impersonality is simply wrong, and this pursuit of quantification at all costs carries significant politi - cal risks. First, not all numerical data are necessarily objec - tive: data can be derived and also read in different ways, and not necessarily objectively. Secondly, this pursuit of quanti - fication at all costs carries the risk that anything that cannot be quantified and cannot be directly translated into a num - ber will be excluded from the political debate. This runs the risk of ignoring the needs and problems of the population and creating disillusionment and distrust of political leaders who seem to systematically ignore anything that cannot be expressed in numbers. Aaron Ben-ze ev , in his article The Crisis of Roman - tic Knowledge: The Role of Information and Ignorance in Times of Romantic Abundance, reflects on how the abun - dance of personal information shared and transmitted on digital dating platforms makes it harder to form solid and lasting romantic relationships. Having so many details about a potential partner does not necessarily make it easier to start a relationship, nor does it increase happiness; instead, the simpler rule of thumb seems to be much more effective in this regard.
